body:
## Summary

`include/UserManager.h` is dead code that stores passwords as plain `std::string` and compares them with `==`. It contradicts the live auth system in `Database.h` (which uses libsodium's `crypto_pwhash`). Its presence is a security hazard — it could be accidentally re-introduced or linked.

## Background

`UserManager.h` (entire file) defines:

```cpp
struct User {
    std::string username;
    std::string password;   // plaintext
    // ...
};

bool authenticate(const std::string& username, const std::string& password) {
    // ...
    return user.password == password;  // direct string comparison — no hashing
}
```

This file is **not included** in any active code path (`Server.h`, `main.cpp`, `server.cpp`). However:

- It exists in the `include/` directory alongside active headers.
- Any developer (or AI assistant) looking for auth code may find it first and assume it's canonical.
- If a future feature accidentally `#include`s it, plaintext password storage silently replaces the secure system.

The active auth system in `Database.h` correctly uses `crypto_pwhash_str` (Argon2id) for hashing and `crypto_pwhash_str_verify` for comparison.

## Proposed fix

Delete the file entirely:

```bash
git rm include/UserManager.h
```

There is no caller. Removing it cannot break any build target. If a `UserManager` abstraction is needed in the future, it should wrap `Database.h`'s secure auth methods.

## Severity

**Medium** — dead code that creates a security trap; no active exploit, but high risk of accidental re-introduction.
title: usermanager-dead-plaintext-password

body:
## Summary

After a fresh login or registration, the post-login snapshot request is sent **without a session token**. The server sees no token, skips setting `current_user_id_`, and the initial `send_user_update()` returns early — so the user's wallet data (cash balance, portfolio) is missing until they perform another action.

## Background

In `App.js` (line 395), after a successful login the frontend sends:

```js
socket.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "snapshot" }));
// Note: no token field
```

In `Server.h` (lines 311–318), the `snapshot` handler only sets `current_user_id_` if a token is present:

```cpp
if (!token.empty()) {
    auto auth = db_.validate_token(token);
    if (auth.ok) current_user_id_ = auth.id;
}
send_snapshot(); // calls send_user_update() internally
```

`send_user_update()` checks `if (current_user_id_ == -1) return;` — so on first login, the wallet update is skipped entirely. The user sees a dashboard with empty/zero balances.

## What breaks

- User registers or logs in for the first time.
- Dashboard loads but shows no cash balance and no portfolio.
- Balance only appears after the next WebSocket round-trip that carries a token (e.g., placing an order).

## Affected files

- `frontend/src/App.js` — line 395
- `include/Server.h` — lines 311–318, 265

## Proposed fix

Include the token in the post-login snapshot request:

```js
// In the logged_in handler:
socket.send(JSON.stringify({
  type: "snapshot",
  token: userData.token   // add this line
}));
```

This is a one-line fix on the frontend. The server already handles a token-bearing snapshot correctly.

## Severity

**Medium** — bad first-impression UX; user sees empty wallet on every fresh login.
title: wallet-missing-on-first-login
open-orders-disappear-on-company-switch

body:
## Summary

Each WebSocket session uses a `std::vector` as a write queue and calls `erase(begin())` to dequeue messages. This is an O(n) operation — every completed write shifts the entire queue. Under broadcast load (every order triggers a book snapshot broadcast to all sessions), this causes quadratic performance degradation.

## Background

In `Server.h`:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> write_queue_;
// ...
write_queue_.erase(write_queue_.begin()); // O(n) — shifts all remaining elements
```

Every time a write completes, all remaining queued messages are shifted left in memory. With N queued messages, each dequeue is O(N). If 100 messages are queued (easily reached during a stress test broadcast), each dequeue scans and moves 99 items.

## What breaks

- Under stress test conditions (thousands of orders/second broadcast to all connected sessions), write throughput drops significantly.
- This affects all connected clients simultaneously since each session has its own queue.
- CPU time is wasted on memory moves instead of actual I/O.

## Affected files

- `include/Server.h` — lines 219–220, 253

## Proposed fix

Replace `std::vector` with `std::deque` for O(1) front removal:

```cpp
// Before:
std::vector<std::string> write_queue_;

// After:
std::deque<std::string> write_queue_;
```

`std::deque::pop_front()` is O(1). The rest of the code (`push_back`, size check, front access) works identically with `std::deque`.

## Severity

**Medium** — performance regression under load; no correctness impact.
title: write-queue-on-dequeue

body:
## Summary

`main.cpp` unconditionally calls `settle_trade(1, 1, 1, 500, 0.0)` on every server startup to seed the demo user's APL shares. Because `create_user` fails silently on restart (user already exists), this settlement runs every time — crediting an additional 500 APL shares to user 1 on each restart.

## Background

The seeding block in `src/main.cpp` (line 22):

```cpp
db.create_user("shrey", "pass123");   // SQLITE_CONSTRAINT on restart — ignored
db.settle_trade(1, 1, 1, 500, 0.0);  // always runs, always credits 500 shares
```

`settle_trade` does an `INSERT OR REPLACE` (or `UPDATE ... SET shares = shares + 500`) which doesn't check whether this is a fresh database. After 10 restarts, user "shrey" has 5,000 APL shares instead of 500.

## What breaks

- Demo user's share balance grows by 500 APL on every server restart.
- On the deployed Azure VM, each redeploy gives "shrey" infinite shares.
- This also sets `price = 0.0` for the seeding trade, which is recorded in trade history as a $0 trade — polluting the trade log.

## Proposed fix

Gate the seeding on whether the user was **freshly created**:

```cpp
auto result = db.create_user("shrey", "pass123");
if (result.ok) {
    // New database — seed initial portfolio
    db.settle_trade(result.id, result.id, 1, 500, 0.0);
}
```

`create_user` should return a struct with `{bool ok, int64_t id}` where `ok` is `true` only when a new user was inserted (not on duplicate).

## Severity

**High** — demo user gets unlimited free shares on every deployment; trade history is polluted.
title: restart-re-seeds-shares

body:
## Summary

The DB worker is designed to wrap a batch of trade settlements in a single SQLite transaction for atomicity. But because `begin_transaction`, each `settle_trade`, and `commit_transaction` each independently acquire and release `db_mutex_`, other threads can interleave reads between individual settlements — exposing partially-settled state to the UI.

## Background

The intended flow in `Server.h` (lines 520–527):

```
db_.begin_transaction()    // acquire + release db_mutex_
for each trade:
    db_.settle_trade(...)  // acquire + release db_mutex_ (per call)
db_.commit_transaction()   // acquire + release db_mutex_
```

Between each `settle_trade` call the mutex is **released**. Any other thread calling `get_user_profile` (to send a wallet update to the UI) can acquire the mutex at that moment and read the database mid-batch — e.g., after cash has been debited but before shares have been credited.

## What breaks

- User's UI flickers: their wallet shows a trade partially applied (wrong cash or wrong share count) for the duration between two `settle_trade` calls.
- In a high-throughput scenario with many simultaneous trades, this window is consistently hit.
- SQLite's WAL mode allows concurrent readers, so this isn't just a theoretical window — readers actively see partial state.

## Affected files

- `include/Database.h` — lines 43–53 (`begin_transaction`, `commit_transaction`)
- `include/Database.h` — lines 222–241 (`settle_trade`)
- `include/Server.h` — lines 520–527 (DB worker batch loop)

## Proposed fix

Hold the lock for the entire batch rather than per-call:

```cpp
void settle_batch(const std::vector<TradeRecord>& trades) {
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(db_mutex_);
    sqlite3_exec(db_, "BEGIN", nullptr, nullptr, nullptr);
    for (const auto& t : trades) {
        settle_trade_unlocked(t); // internal version that doesn't re-lock
    }
    sqlite3_exec(db_, "COMMIT", nullptr, nullptr, nullptr);
}
```

Add `settle_trade_unlocked` as an internal method that assumes the lock is already held.

## Severity

**High** — users see incorrect, inconsistent wallet state during active trading.
title: broken-batch-db-transaction

body:
## Summary

`cancel_order` uses the `price` value sent by the client to select which price-level list to modify — but never verifies this matches the actual stored price. A mismatched price (accidental or malicious) corrupts a completely unrelated price level in the order book.

## Background

`cancel_order(bool side, uint32_t price, uint64_t order_id, int64_t user_id)` in `OrderBook.h`:

1. Retrieves the node via `order_map_array_[order_id % MAX_ORDERS]`.
2. Validates `node.order.id`, `node.order.user_id`, and `node.order.side`.
3. Uses the **client-supplied `price`** to pick the list: `OrderList& list = side ? bids_[price] : asks_[price];`
4. Proceeds to unlink the node from that list.

If the `price` sent by the client differs from the node's actual `node.order.price`, the function modifies the wrong `OrderList` — corrupting `head_idx`, `tail_idx`, `total_quantity`, and `order_count` of an unrelated price level.

## What breaks

- A user sends a cancel with the correct `order_id` but a wrong `price` (e.g., off by 1 cent).
- The node is found and passes user/side validation.
- The wrong price level's linked list is surgically corrupted — removing a node that doesn't belong to it.
- Other users' orders at that price level may become unreachable or produce incorrect total quantities.

## Affected files

- `include/OrderBook.h` — lines 103–129

## Proposed fix

After retrieving the node, verify the price matches before using it:

```cpp
// Add this check after validating id/user_id/side:
if (node.order.price != price) return false;
```

Better yet, don't take `price` as a parameter at all — read it directly from the node:

```cpp
uint32_t actual_price = node.order.price;
OrderList& list = side ? bids_[actual_price] : asks_[actual_price];
```

This way the client-supplied price is only used for the initial lookup (or can be dropped entirely).

## Severity

**High** — corrupts unrelated price levels; can be triggered accidentally or deliberately.
title: cancel-wrong-price-level-corruption

body:
## Summary

When an order is partially filled and then cancelled (or simply never fully filled), the over-reserved cash or shares are **never refunded**. The user permanently loses the balance for the unfilled portion.

## Background

The reservation system works like this:

- BUY order for `qty` shares at `price`: `reserve_cash(user_id, price * qty)` deducts the **full** amount upfront.
- SELL order for `qty` shares: `reserve_shares(user_id, company_id, qty)` deducts the **full** quantity upfront.

`settle_trade` only credits the **filled** portion. There is no code path that refunds the **unfilled** remainder when:
- An order is partially filled and the rest is cancelled.
- A resting order is cancelled before it fills at all.

## What breaks

**Example:**
1. User places BUY 1000 shares @ $50 → $50,000 reserved.
2. Only 300 shares are filled (matched against incoming sell orders).
3. User cancels the remaining 700 shares.
4. `cancel_order` removes the node from the book successfully.
5. **No refund is issued.** The $35,000 for the 700 unfilled shares is gone from the user's balance permanently.

The same applies symmetrically for partial sell orders.

## Affected files

- `include/Database.h` — lines 222–241 (`settle_trade` — no refund logic)
- `include/Server.h` — lines 360–367 (reservation on order submit)
- `include/OrderBook.h` — `cancel_order` return path (no refund trigger)

## Proposed fix

1. Add refund helpers to `Database.h`:

```cpp
void release_cash(int64_t user_id, int64_t amount_cents);
void release_shares(int64_t user_id, int company_id, int64_t quantity);
```

2. In the engine worker's cancel handler, after a successful `cancel_order`, post a DB task:

```cpp
// if cancelled order was a buy:
db_.release_cash(user_id, cancelled_order.price * cancelled_order.remaining_qty);
// if cancelled order was a sell:
db_.release_shares(user_id, company_id, cancelled_order.remaining_qty);
```

3. Also track `remaining_qty` on each `OrderNode` so the correct unfilled amount is refunded.

## Severity

**Critical** — every partial fill or cancellation silently steals funds from users. No notification, no recovery.
title: partial-fill-cancel-no-refund

body:
## Summary

A user can trade against their own resting orders. There is no `user_id` check before executing a match, enabling wash trades — fake volume and potential balance manipulation.

## Background

In `match_buy` and `match_sell` (`OrderBook.h`), when an incoming order matches a resting order at the same price, `execute_match` is called immediately. There is no check that `incoming.user_id != resting.user_id`.

## What breaks

**Scenario:**
1. User A places a SELL order: 100 shares of APL at $50. Shares are reserved.
2. User A places a BUY order: 100 shares of APL at $50. Cash is reserved.
3. The engine matches them — a trade fires between User A and User A.
4. Settlement credits User A's cash (from the sell side) and shares (from the buy side).
5. Net result: User A ends up with the same shares and nearly the same cash, but a trade was recorded — fake volume on the book.

In edge cases with partial fills and rounding, this can also produce a net gain in balance.

This is a **wash trade** — illegal on real exchanges and a sign of market manipulation.

## Affected files

- `include/OrderBook.h` — lines 323–374 (`match_buy`, `match_sell`, `execute_match`)

## Proposed fix

Add a self-trade check inside `execute_match` (or at the top of the matching loop):

```cpp
// Cancel-on-self: if the resting order belongs to the same user, abort the match
if (incoming.user_id == resting_node.order.user_id) {
    // send error notification to session, stop matching
    break;
}
```

Alternatively, use skip-on-self (skip that resting order and continue to the next). For this project, cancel-on-self with an error response to the client is the simplest correct behaviour.

## Severity

**Critical** — allows fake volume generation and potential balance manipulation.
title: self-trade-not-prevented

body:
## Summary

When the order pool is full, new orders are silently dropped — but the user's cash or shares have **already been reserved** before the drop. The funds are never refunded, effectively stealing money from the user.

## Background

The server flow for a new order is:

1. `Server.h` calls `db_.reserve_cash(...)` or `db_.reserve_shares(...)` — this **immediately deducts** from the user's balance.
2. The order is pushed as an `EngineTask` to the SPSC queue.
3. The engine thread calls `add_order` → `insert_to_book`.
4. If `free_indices_` (the pool) is empty, `insert_to_book` prints to `stderr` and **returns without inserting**.

There is no rollback path. The reservation is permanent.

## What breaks

- User places a buy order for 100 shares at $50 → $5,000 is deducted from their balance.
- Pool is full → order is silently dropped.
- User's balance shows −$5,000 with no order in the book and no trade executed.
- No error message is sent to the client.

## Affected files

- `include/OrderBook.h` — lines 293–296 (`insert_to_book` failure path)
- `include/Server.h` — lines 360–367 (reservation before engine push)

## Proposed fix

1. `insert_to_book` should return a `bool` indicating success/failure.
2. `add_order` should propagate that failure back to the engine worker.
3. The engine worker, on failure, should post a DB task to call `release_cash` / `release_shares` to refund the reservation.
4. An error response should be sent to the client's WebSocket session.

```cpp
// New refund helpers in Database.h
void release_cash(int64_t user_id, int64_t amount);
void release_shares(int64_t user_id, int company_id, int64_t quantity);
```

## Severity

**Critical** — user funds are permanently lost with no notification and no recovery path.
title: pool-exhaustion-funds-stolen

body:
## Summary

After 1,000,000 cumulative orders are submitted to the server (across its lifetime), new order IDs collide with old ones in the order map array. This silently overwrites live resting orders, permanently breaking the ability to cancel them and leaking pool slots forever.

## Background

`order_map_array_` in `OrderBook.h` is a fixed-size array of 1,000,000 slots indexed by `order_id % MAX_ORDERS`. `order_id` is a monotonically increasing `uint64_t` that **never resets** between server restarts (it's persisted via the DB). Once order ID 1,000,001 arrives, it maps to slot 1 — the same slot as order ID 1.

## What breaks

- If the old order in that slot is still resting in the book, `insert_to_book` overwrites `order_map_array_[slot]` with the new order's index.
- The old order becomes an **orphan**: it occupies a pool slot forever (pool leak) and its price-level linked list is corrupted because `cancel_order` can no longer find it via the map.
- The user who placed the old order can never cancel it. Their reserved funds are locked permanently.

## Affected files

- `include/OrderBook.h` — lines 104, 306, 370

## Steps to reproduce

1. Submit 1,000,001 orders to the server without restarting.
2. Order ID 1,000,001 maps to slot 1. If order ID 1 is still resting, it is silently overwritten.
3. Attempt to cancel order ID 1 — the cancel silently fails or operates on the wrong node.

## Proposed fix

Replace the open-addressing array with a proper hash map:

```cpp
// instead of:
uint32_t order_map_array_[MAX_ORDERS];

// use:
std::unordered_map<uint64_t, uint32_t> order_map_;
```

At minimum, add a collision guard in `insert_to_book`: if the slot is already occupied by a different live order ID, log and reject the new order rather than silently corrupting state.

## Severity

**Critical** — silent data corruption after a reachable usage threshold; no crash, no log entry, no user notification.

comments.body:
First of all, I'd like to point out that we should decrease MAX_ORDERS from 1 million to 100,000. This allows the entire array of 100,000 elements to fit into the CPU's L3 cache, it is still more than enough open orders, and it models real exchange engines better.

Coming to the above mentioned issue, there is a better way than hash map (std::unordered_map) to solve this issue. I have the following idea:

We can delegate the responsibility of assigning order IDs to the server (currently the order book is responsible), and give the server access to the "free_indices" stack.

The least significant 32 bits of the order ID would store the index of the order (obtained by popping from free_indices stack), and the most significant 32 bits of the order ID would store a global counter which increments every time an order is created (with wraparound allowed). Storing the index as part of the order ID allows us to access the order in worst case O(1) time, as opposed to the hash map solution which is average case O(1). 

On first glance, it may seem unnecessary to store a global counter as part of the order ID, if we are already storing the index which can differentiate between all open orders. However, due to race conditions (decided not to delve into in this comment), it becomes important to check whether an order being cancelled is indeed the correct order to cancel or not.

title: order-map-hash-collision
